item.title: Mañenggon Memorial Foundation will hold ‘Christmases Not Forgotten’ for WWII survivors

item.content:encoded:
The Mañenggon Memorial Foundation will host Christmases Not Forgotten, a gathering honoring Guam’s World War II survivors who missed out on celebrating Christmas during the Japanese occupation.

The event is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Dec. 6 at the Zefiro Ballroom at LeoPalace Resort. It will bring together manåmko’ and their families for an afternoon of fellowship, music, dining, and honoring those whose lives were lost and those who survived WWII.

The Christmases Not Forgotten was created by a committee of the Mañenggon Memorial Foundation, including war survivor advisors Julia Villagomez, Rosa “Tan Chai” Duenas and David D.L. Flores. Foundation founders Willy Flores and Rita Franquez organized the gathering after hearing survivors share their experiences during and after the war. Flores said many survivors recalled missing family being together and gatherings of Christmas celebrations between 1941 and 1944.

Flores and Franquez said survivors recalled that during the war, some were able to say nobenas, or the CHamoru rosary, in secret.

“They could not get together openly, and they definitely could not celebrate Christmas,” Flores said. “They talked about how Christmas was taken from them in 1941, then of course 42, 43, and then 44. Even though the island was basically freed in July and August, still there was no time to put together Christmas in 44.”

The gathering will include live entertainment, a special surprise appearance, a visit from Santa Claus, gifts, and a shared meal. The foundation said their goal is to honor and celebrate the manåmko’ of Guam and those who have survived and lost their lives in WWII.

Admission is free for Guam WWII survivors. Individual tickets are $65. Family tables and corporate sponsorship opportunities are also available.

The foundation hopes the gathering will help preserve their stories and ensure future generations understand the experiences and sacrifices of those who lived through the war.

item.content:encoded:
CNMI Delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds has requested a briefing from the U.S. Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, to discuss concerns about illicit financial activity and the potential role of Chinese money laundering networks in the Commonwealth.

In a Nov. 18 letter to FinCEN acting Director Jenna Casanova, King-Hinds said federal investigations and prosecutions over the years have highlighted concerns about money laundering and other financial crimes linked to Chinese capital in the CNMI.

The delegate said more information is needed to understand how such networks operate, whether they remain active in the Northern Marianas and what steps federal and local officials can take to address potential risks.

King-Hinds requested a briefing with FinCEN officials to identify vulnerabilities that could be exploited by criminal organizations and to explore possible legislative, regulatory and enforcement measures to strengthen prevention efforts.

She said the CNMI's proximity to East Asia, its integration into the U.S. financial system and its economic ties to the region warrant closer examination of financial crime risks.

King-Hinds said protecting legitimate investment and economic activity while preventing illicit financial networks from exploiting local institutions is critical to the Commonwealth's economic and security interests.

item.content:encoded:
Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero has declared the day after Thanksgiving - Black Friday - a government of Guam holiday, giving government employees an additional day off this week

In an executive order issued Monday, Leon Guerrero designated Nov. 27 as a government holiday. All executive branch departments and agencies will be closed that day, with the exception of essential personnel and operations deemed necessary by agency heads to protect public health, safety and welfare.

The governor said the additional holiday recognizes the work of public servants while allowing families more time to spend together during the holiday season.

Lt. Gov. Joshua Tenorio also encouraged residents to support local businesses over the extended holiday weekend and practice inafa’maolek by looking out for one another on the roads and in their neighborhoods.

Residents are encouraged to plan ahead for any government services they may need before the Friday closure.

item.content:encoded:
BUNIA, Congo — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus , for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation .

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises . The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

item.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
item.description: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia. item.content:encoded:
SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.

Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.

KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South Korea Kim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.

"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.

Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.

Trump still hopes to meet Kim Trump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.

In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."

Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."

Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.

Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."

Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

item.title: 'Memories of a Good Meal': How food made a difference during WWII
item.description: NEW ORLEANS — Chef Alon Shaya believes there's power in a meal. "It's always been the way that I can start a conversation, build a relationship, disagree about things, but still be able to come together and break bread," Shaya, of the acclaimed Crescent City restaurant Saba, said one recent afternoon. "When you share a meal with someone, a lot of those barriers get broken down."
item.content:encoded:
NEW ORLEANS — Chef Alon Shaya believes there's power in a meal.

"It's always been the way that I can start a conversation, build a relationship, disagree about things, but still be able to come together and break bread," Shaya, of the acclaimed Crescent City restaurant Saba, said one recent afternoon. "When you share a meal with someone, a lot of those barriers get broken down."

The Israeli American chef also believes food can be a source of inspiration even in the darkest of times. A few years ago, he spearheaded the Rescued Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and that got him digging deeper into the role that food played during World War II.

Now, he's collected those stories and the dishes they inspired in a new historical cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival .

Shaya hopes home cooks use the recipes to inspire dinner table conversations about the deeper stories behind them.

"I want people to gather and cook and eat and put their phones down, and share a meal and recount these miraculous stories of survival, resilience and heroism," he told NPR.

Stories like that of Roddie Edmonds, a U.S. Army master sergeant, whose unit was captured in the Battle of the Bulge and imprisoned in a German POW camp. (Edmonds posthumously won the Congressional Medal of Honor earlier this year for his refusal to turn in his Jewish troops to be sent to concentration camps.)

One of the ways Edmonds and his fellow prisoners distracted themselves from the horror of the camp was to talk about the foods that reminded them of home, be it Sunday spaghetti sauce, hot cakes or cherry pie.

"They're eating up this idea that they were going to go home," Shaya said. "They were going to be free, and they were going to be able to sit around and dig into that filet mignon with creamy mushroom sauce."

The servicemen sketched out detailed plans for a dreamed-of restaurant called the Jolly Chef. There, they would serve all those yearned-for dishes, including candied yams with pecans and whipped marshmallow — one of the recipes in the new cookbook.

Another chapter highlights Polish partisan fighters who lived in underground bunkers and sabotaged the Nazis by derailing trains and blowing up ammunition plants. In a nod to the fire that ensued, a recipe from their chapter also includes smashed potatoes flambéed in vodka.

"Vodka was a form of currency for them," Shaya said. "They would use it to barter. They would use it to celebrate. And so each moment of that recipe helps to really tell the story of what they were going through."

The book has stories from around the world – Hungarian Jews whose non-Jewish cook salvaged the treasured family cookbook as they were being sent to Auschwitz; a French village that took in Jewish children and hid them from the Nazis; Navajo code breakers who changed the course of the war; and Japanese Americans, convicted of no crimes, who were incarcerated in military-style camps in the U.S.

June Hersh , a food historian and writer who worked with Shaya on the cookbook, said remembering and talking about favorite recipes was a form of resistance – turning a tragic situation into something triumphant.

"You can put me in a uniform, you can make me do hard labor, you can shave my head, you can starve me if you want, but I'm not going to let go of my food memory," she said. "It's something you can't take away from me."

item.title: At Albuquerque's Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course

item.content:encoded:
There are plenty of kitschy diners and barbecue joints along Route 66, but just a couple of miles off the highway in Albuquerque, N.M., Native American dishes are the star at Indian Pueblo Kitchen .

Late on a weekday morning, the restaurant was already starting to fill up. Most of the tables were taken up by locals, like Merlyn Liberty and Rolf Pendall.

"I started with breakfast dessert. The blue corn waffles. And now I'm finishing up my sweetheart's plate of enchiladas and pinto beans," Pendall said.

The restaurant is attached to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center , a museum and cultural center founded in 1976 by the 19 Pueblo tribes of New Mexico.

The center sits on land where the Albuquerque Indian School operated. Open from 1881 to the early 1980s, it was one of the hundreds of federally funded boarding schools designed to strip Native American children of their family bonds, languages, culture and spiritual practices.

The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center's president and CEO, Monique Fragua, said visitors can start in the museum's galleries and then visit the restaurant to experience Pueblo culture and hospitality.

"Whether that's through our exhibits, or our food, or in our gift shop, we can celebrate the art of our Pueblo communities," Fragua said.

Museum cafés are not a typical destination for foodies, but this one is.

The menu is all Native American and Southwestern-inspired. Dishes include blue corn enchiladas that you can get "Christmas style," one with red chile sauce and the other with green chile sauce. There's a chile posole with beef short ribs served on the bone, as well as Indian tacos on homemade fry bread. Then there's a dish that's really popular on social media : pickles marinated in cherry Kool-Aid and then deep-fried and served with a green chile ranch sauce.

Rita Toledo, from Jemez Pueblo, is Indian Pueblo Kitchen's star baker. One of her specialties is biscochitos — fragrant shortbread cookies spiced with anise and rolled in cinnamon sugar that are New Mexico's state cookie. Toledo has made some twists on the traditional biscochito, like making a chile pepper version that has just a little kick at the end with a nice balance of sweet and heat.

Indian Pueblo Kitchen's version of biscochitos is so popular that the restaurant also sells them at its café inside Albuquerque's airport. Toledo turns out at least 48 dozen biscochitos each week just for the airport location.

While we chatted, Toledo was wrestling to open a giant tub of one of her main ingredients — lard. These cookies can be made with butter or shortening, she said, but "lard's the only way to make good biscochitos."

Toledo said that she has been baking all her life and that her favorite part of her work is rolling out dough.

"It calms me. You know, your energy comes out on your dough," Toledo said. "I always tell my bakers, 'Come in happy and in a good mood. That way, your products will come out nice and everybody's gonna love it.'"

Along with locals flocking to visit, the restaurant is also a hit with tourists like Kathy Allio and Jeff Allen from Pennsylvania. While we chatted, Allio was finishing a bowl of bean chili with elk meat.

"The red chiles are just very flavorful without being hot," Allio said, "so it's delicious."

One thing Fragua, the center's president, is particularly proud of is that the Pueblo community can see itself reflected in the museum's galleries and programming and on the restaurant's menu.

"We're lucky to have that history here on our campus, that we've taken lands that were once created to really change the identity of Native people and change that story of who Native people are," Fragua said. "We've created a campus that's built on resilience, empowering our voices and truly telling the stories of who we are as Native people."

Additional reporting by Jeanette DeDios of member station KUNM.
